query: Consider noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles containing more than five elements and targeted in a single-phase solid-solution state. Their crystal structure is difficult to control at fixed composition, while unsuccessful formation can involve phase separation, elemental segregation, uncontrolled particle morphology, and high thermal decomposition temperatures under synthesis regimes with rapid heating and cooling. What testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs formation and crystal-structure selection in this regime and why? Define a controlled intervention without specifying a technique, predict the observations relative to the initial single-phase baseline, identify the applicable compositional and processing boundaries, cite supporting evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: For sub-10 nm noble-metal high-entropy alloy (HEA) nanoparticles that nominally contain ≥6 near-equiatomic late–transition elements (e.g., Ag–Au–Pd–Pt–Ir–Cu), the selection of a single-phase fcc solid solution versus phase-separated or polymorphic products is governed primarily by the competition between (i) element-specific surface-segregation enthalpies that favor demixing and (ii) bulk configurational entropy that favors random mixing. If the surface free-energy differences among the elements are equalized during nucleation—by adsorbing a common strongly binding, soft donor ligand that complexes each metal with comparable strength—then the surface-segregation driving force is quenched, tipping the balance toward the entropy-stabilized single-phase fcc structure at a given synthesis temperature.
generation.material_initial_state: Colloidally prepared ∼5 ± 2 nm alloy nanoparticles containing Ag, Au, Pd, Pt, Ir, and Cu in equiatomic atomic ratio, generated in a polyol medium under rapid heating (≈10 °C s⁻¹) and capped only with weakly binding solvent molecules (no added strong ligands); baseline product shows partial elemental segregation and mixed fcc + amorphous domains.
generation.intervention: Introduce during synthesis a stoichiometric excess (≥10× total metal atom concentration) of a soft donor, isovalent ligand (e.g., aliphatic thiols or phosphines) that adsorbs with comparable binding energy (<15 kJ mol⁻¹ variation) to all six metal surfaces, while leaving all other synthesis parameters unchanged.
generation.conditions: Solution-phase reduction at 180 °C for 30 min under inert atmosphere; identical heating/cooling ramps (≈10 °C s⁻¹) for control and ligand-treated batches.
generation.structural_mediator: Ligand-induced reduction of inter-element surface-energy differences, suppressing preferential surface segregation during nucleation and growth.
generation.mechanism: In the absence of strongly binding, non-selective ligands, elements with lower surface energy (e.g., Ag, Au) preferentially segregate to the nanoparticle surface during rapid growth, locally depleting high-surface-energy elements (e.g., Pt, Ir) from the interface. This segregation lowers the overall Gibbs free energy and seeds compositionally distinct regions that evolve into multiphase or core–shell structures upon subsequent ripening. Introducing a strongly binding ligand that coordinates each element equally raises and homogenizes the surface free energy landscape (γ_i → γ̄), diminishing the enthalpic driving force for segregation. Because the nanoparticles are <10 nm, the configurational entropy term (TΔS_conf ≈ 0.2–0.3 eV atom⁻¹ at 180 °C) then dominates, stabilizing a homogeneous fcc solid solution that persists on cooling despite the rapid quench.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline, ligand-treated particles will exhibit (1) a single set of fcc diffraction peaks (XRD, SAED) without extra reflections, (2) no statistically significant elemental segregation in atomic-resolution STEM-EDX/EELS maps (composition variance <5 % across the particle), and (3) lower onset temperature for crystallographic decomposition upon post-synthesis annealing (DSC/TEM).
generation.baseline: Control synthesis lacking strong, non-selective ligands yields partially phase-segregated nanoparticles displaying multiple crystalline domains (fcc + amorphous or hcp) and ≥15 % radial composition gradients (surface Au/Ag enrichment) detected by STEM-EDX line scans.
generation.boundary: Effect expected for particle diameters ≤10 nm, total standard deviation of elemental surface energies ≥0.3 J m⁻², and processing temperatures between 150–250 °C. Outside this size range (>15 nm) or for elements with nearly identical surface energies (<0.1 J m⁻²), the intervention should have negligible impact.
generation.uncertainty: Direct calorimetric data on ligand-modified surface energies are limited; other kinetic factors (e.g., reduction rate) might also influence mixing, so the predicted magnitude of segregation suppression (≤5 % compositional variance) is uncertain within ±3 %.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two nanoparticle batches at the stated composition and temperature ramp: (A) control with only solvent/weak capping species; (B) identical but with the specified equimolar soft-ligand additive. Characterize freshly isolated particles and after annealing at 300 °C for 1 h under inert gas.
measurements: Powder X-ray diffraction (peak positions, widths, and extra reflections)
Atomic-resolution STEM-HAADF imaging with EDX/EELS elemental maps (quantitative compositional variance)
Differential scanning calorimetry during annealing (exotherms corresponding to phase separation)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if, under the ligand treatment (B), (i) more than one crystalline phase is detected by XRD/SAED, OR (ii) STEM-EDX line scans reveal radial or domain-level elemental segregation exceeding 10 % relative variation, OR (iii) the onset temperature for decomposition is not shifted to lower values relative to control. Any one of these outcomes would refute the proposed mechanism that equalizing surface energies via non-selective ligands stabilizes the single-phase fcc HEA nanoparticles.
